Homovanillic acid is a catecholamine metabolite excreted in urine. In a chart review of ganglioneuromas, raised values appeared to become more common with larger tumors, which points to the tumor as their source, though the authors report this only as a trend; they advise a search for occult neuroblastoma, which can be the source instead, when values are extremely high.
intermediate_mechanisms: Metabolism of the secreted catecholamines to homovanillic acid and its excretion in urine

nodes.description: Differentiation of neuroblastic cells into ganglion cells. Biologically favorable peripheral neuroblastic tumors are considered to mature by age-dependent steps from neuroblastoma through intermixed ganglioneuroblastoma to ganglioneuroma. In German trials of localized tumors, median age at diagnosis rose with the grade of differentiation, which the authors read as indirect support for tumors maturing in situ. Whether every ganglioneuroma arises this way is unproven (discussion gn_origin).

This is in line with the theory that mature NT might just have had enough time to mature in situ before they were discovered.

The figure is the share of patients whose diagnosis was prompted by pain, and the frequent band rests on this one cohort of young patients.

nodes.description: The Schwann-cell stroma that dominates ganglioneuroma tissue; the INPC names ganglioneuroma for this feature (Schwannian stroma-dominant). Stromal Schwann cells in ganglioneuroma share the expression of nerve repair-associated genes with the repair Schwann cells of human nerve injured ex vivo, and repair-type Schwann cells and their secretome induce neuronal differentiation of neuroblastoma cells in culture. It has been suggested that a minor increase in the volume of mature tumors may also be caused by proliferation of the Schwannian stroma rather than of tumor cells. Whether the stromal cells derive from the neoplastic clone is discussed in the Ganglioneuroblastoma entry.

evidence.reference_title: Terminology and morphologic criteria of neuroblastic tumors: recommendations by the International Neuroblastoma Pathology Committee.
evidence.snippet: Based on morphologic criteria defined in this article, NTs were classified into four categories and their subtypes: 1) neuroblastoma (Schwannian stroma-poor), undifferentiated, poorly differentiated, and differentiating; 2) ganglioneuroblastoma, intermixed (Schwannian stroma-rich); 3) ganglioneuroma (Schwannian stroma-dominant), maturing and mature; and 4) ganglioneuroblastoma, nodular (composite Schwannian stroma-richlstroma-dominant and stroma-poor).

nodes.description: In German trials of localized tumors in patients aged 21 years or younger, no ganglioneuroma or intermixed ganglioneuroblastoma progressed after complete resection or with residuals under 2 cm, and incomplete resection leaving minor residuals appeared to be sufficient treatment; the 11 patients given chemotherapy, 2 of them with ganglioneuroma, showed no substantial effect, and the authors' conclusion that chemotherapy is not effective pools the two tumor types. Postoperative complications are common: short-term complications followed 43.1% of operations, most often neurological deficits (22.2%), in a 101-patient single-institution series; complications followed surgery in 11 of 51 patients (21.6%) with a resected retroperitoneal ganglioneuroma at a sarcoma center, one of whom died on postoperative day 8 of bowel ischemia; post-operative complications occurred in 15 of 50 surgical patients (30%) in a pediatric series, and a UK nationwide series reported a 19% complication rate, both pooling ganglioneuroma with intermixed ganglioneuroblastoma. In two children with a VIP-secreting ganglioneuroma, VIP returned to normal after the operation and the diarrhea stopped.

evidence.reference_title: Treatment and outcome of Ganglioneuroma and Ganglioneuroblastoma intermixed.
evidence.snippet: Outcome was excellent and chemotherapy seems not effective while incomplete resection with minor residuals (<2 cm) appears to be sufficient for treatment.

One patient with GN presented with a large stage 3 tumor and received chemotherapy because diagnosis of GN was made only from biopsy and immature components within the residuals were suspected by local physicians. The other patient with GN received chemotherapy because of an intraspinal tumor mass. No patient showed significant response to chemotherapy and residual tumor is still observed.

nodes.description: Secretion of catecholamines by the tumor, which some ganglioneuromas show. In a series of primary ganglioneuromas, plasma and/or urinary catecholamines were increased in 39%, and the authors concluded that ganglioneuroma may present with increased catecholamine secretion; in an adrenal ganglioneuroma, raised urinary catecholamines normalized after resection, which the authors took as confirming the tumor as their source. Secretion is not universal: the authors of an adrenal series concluded that isolated adrenal ganglioneuromas do not produce catecholamines. In a chart review, raised urinary vanillylmandelic and homovanillic acid appeared to become more common with larger ganglioneuromas, and the authors advised a search for occult neuroblastoma when the values are extremely high.

nodes.description: Secretion of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) by the tumor, described in case reports of young children with ganglioneuroma and diarrhea. In one child with a retroperitoneal tumor, the tumor contained large amounts of VIP, plasma VIP was raised before surgery and the VIP concentration was normal after it; in a child with a thoracic tumor, the authors attributed the diarrhea to an excess of VIP secreted by the tumor; and in a 3-year-old girl with a thoracic paraspinal tumor, serum VIP was 314 pmol/l before surgery (normal less than 30) and 14 pmol/l 6 months after it.

evidence.reference_title: Vasocative intestinal polypeptide (VIP)-producing ganglioneuroma in a child with chronic diarrhea.
evidence.snippet: The tumour contained large amounts of vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) and preoperative plasma concentration of this peptide was increased. Postoperatively the VIP concentration was normalized, and the diarrhea ceased. Analysis of catecholamine metabolites in urine was normal. The findings suggest that the watery diarrhea was due to the benign VIP-producing neural crest tumour.
